title: A Walk That Visits Every Free Square Once

concept.title: Count the squares you have walked on, and compare at the end
body: The grid has a start square (`1`), an end square (`2`), free squares (`0`) and walls (`-1`). You want the number of walks from the start to the end that visit **every non-wall square exactly once**. A depth-first search with marking does the walking. The new element is the **end test**: when the walk arrives at the end square, it is a success only if the number of visited squares equals the number of all non-wall squares.

Turning a visited square into a wall (and restoring the old value afterwards) is a handy way to avoid a second table. A walk that reaches the end too early simply gives 0 and does not continue: the end square is the last one. With at most 20 squares the number of walks to explore is small.

statement: A grid has squares with these values: `1` the start (exactly one), `2` the end (exactly one), `0` a free square and `-1` a wall. In one move you go to a neighbouring square (above, below, left or right) that is not a wall. Count the walks from the start to the end that step on every non-wall square exactly once.
inputFormat: Each of the next `r` lines has `c` integers.
constraints: Every value is -1, 0, 1 or 2; there is exactly one 1 and exactly one 2.

examples.note: There are two walks that cover all 11 non-wall squares.

hints: Count the squares walked so far; at the end square compare it with the total.
Mark a square by changing its value, and restore the value when the search comes back.

r, c = map(int, input().split())
g = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(r)]

explanation: The walk marks each visited square as a wall and counts the visited squares. At the end square it counts one only when all non-wall squares were visited; every square is restored when the search backs out.
solution.complexity: Time exponential but tiny for 20 squares, space O(r * c).
